content: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is an extremely common virus that can lead to the development of certain cancers later in life. Vaccination against HPV is a highly effective way to protect children from these cancers. Without vaccination, nearly everyone will contract HPV at some point in their lifetime. HPV infections are widespread, with over 42 million Americans currently infected with HPV types that are known to cause disease. Each year, approximately 13 million new infections occur in the United States, including among teenagers. The virus is transmitted through intimate skin-to-skin contact, including vaginal, anal, or oral sex, even if the infected individual shows no symptoms or signs of the virus. HPV is categorized into two main types: non-oncogenic types, which cause warts, and oncogenic types, which are associated with an increased risk of cancer. Oncogenic HPV types can lead to cancers of the cervix, vagina, vulva, penis, anus, and the oropharynx (the back of the throat, including the base of the tongue and tonsils). In the United States, HPV is responsible for approximately 36,000 cases of cancer annually in both men and women. In most cases, HPV infections resolve on their own within two years. However, in some instances, the infection persists and can lead to the development of cancer over time. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) strongly recommends HPV vaccination to protect against these risks. The vaccine is most effective when administered before exposure to the virus. The recommended vaccination schedule involves two doses for children aged 11–12 years, though vaccination can begin as early as age 9. If the first dose is given before the child’s 15th birthday, only two doses are required. However, if the first dose is administered on or after the 15th birthday, three doses are necessary to ensure full protection.
